content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis (TB) treatment, specifically focusing on drug-resistant TB. These guidelines, updated in 2022, are part of Module 4 and include detailed recommendations for treatment regimens. The guidelines are available electronically under ISBN 978-92-4-006398-3 and are distributed under a Creative Commons license, allowing for non-commercial use, adaptation, and redistribution, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or equivalent Creative Commons license. Translations of the guidelines must include a disclaimer stating that WHO is not responsible for the content or accuracy of the translation, and the original English version remains the authoritative edition. The guidelines were developed following internationally recognized standards, such as the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach, to ensure a structured and transparent methodology for policymaking. A WHO Guideline Steering Group identified areas requiring updated evidence and coordinated the involvement of experts to synthesize and review new data. An external review group also evaluated the updated recommendations. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) included researchers, epidemiologists, clinicians, national TB program officers, community representatives, and evidence synthesis experts. Declarations of interest (DOI) were managed according to WHO's Conflict of Interest Policy, and the full list of GDG members and their biographies were published online for transparency. The GDG met virtually in early 2022 to discuss and reach consensus on recommendations. When consensus could not be achieved through discussion, decisions were made by majority vote. The GRADE approach was used to assess the certainty of evidence (rated as high, moderate, low, or very low) and the strength of recommendations (strong or conditional). A scoping proposal was approved by the WHO Guideline Review Committee, and public comments were solicited to ensure transparency and address any potential conflicts of interest. The guidelines focus on evaluating novel treatment regimens for multidrug-resistant (MDR) and rifampicin-resistant (RR) TB. Key questions addressed by the GDG included the use of shorter all-oral regimens, the inclusion of specific medications such as bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid, and the effectiveness of these regimens in various patient populations, including those with fluoroquinolone resistance or pre-extensively drug-resistant (pre-XDR) TB. The outcomes of interest included sustained treatment success, treatment failure, recurrence, mortality, loss to follow-up, adverse events, and the development of additional drug resistance. Evidence for these recommendations was derived from clinical trials such as the TB-PRACTECAL, ZeNix, and Nix-TB studies, as well as programmatic data from national TB programs in countries like South Africa. Additional data were provided by cohort studies and other trials, such as the NExT trial, which evaluated a 6–9-month all-oral regimen for MDR-TB in South Africa. However, the GDG decided not to use data from the NExT trial due to its early termination and variability in the intervention regimen components. The guidelines aim to provide updated, evidence-based recommendations for the treatment of drug-resistant TB, ensuring transparency and adherence to rigorous methodological standards.
